Question six. Why are dict and set lookups order one, and when does that matter? A list doesn't know where a value lives, so a membership test compares from the front: a million comparisons for the last of a million numbers. Dicts and sets are hash tables. Hashing the value picks one bucket out of two million, and Python goes straight there: one comparison, at any size. Timed in CPython, that's five and a half milliseconds, against twenty-three nanoseconds. It matters inside a loop. Deduplicate ten thousand records against a list of the ones you've seen: fifty million comparisons. Double the records, and it's four times as many, order n squared. A set makes it one lookup a record. So, deduplicating.

Question seven. How do you deduplicate records in memory? One pass, with a set of the keys you've seen. User one's second record is skipped, and each user's first is kept, in order: one, two, three. To keep the latest instead, map each key to a record in a dict, and replace it when a later timestamp arrives. Question eight. How do you keep only the latest record per key in pandas? Sort by timestamp, drop duplicates on the key, and keep the last. ID one keeps b, from time twenty: the pandas version of row number equals one in sequel. If two rows can share a timestamp, add a tiebreaker to the sort, so which one you keep doesn't depend on arrival order. A dict can do a join, too.
